title: Read a fuel heater's label before it goes in a room
summary: Two heaters that look alike can be one rated for a room and one that will poison it. The label's use statement, the certification mark and the standard it names tell you which, and how much fresh air it needs. Treat any heater without a readable label as outdoor only.

steps.text: Find the rating plate or label: on the back, the base, inside the cylinder door or under the fuel cap. Read the model number, fuel, heat output (Btu/h or kW), the certification mark and the use statement. Photograph it.

Read the use statement first. 'Not for home or recreational vehicle use' means a construction heater. 'Outdoor use only' means never inside anything with a roof and walls. 'Indoor use' always comes with a ventilation condition: find it.
steps.warn: An oxygen sensor, a tip-over switch or a cabinet that looks like a home heater does not make a heater safe indoors. Only the label and manual decide.

steps.text: Check the mark covers Canada. On an ETL mark, 'us' alone means US standards only and a small 'c' means Canadian (Intertek ETL guide); other marks use their own symbols, so read the maker's instructions for where the heater may be used. The same model number can come with an indoor-use manual in the US and an outdoor-only manual in Canada: the MH9BX Portable Buddy's US manual allows emergency indoor use, and its Canada-sale manual says outdoor use only (Mr. Heater MH9BX, Mr. Heater MH9BX CAN).

Look for the safety devices: an ODS pilot with a thermocouple at the burner, a tip-over switch on gas heaters, an automatic extinguisher on kerosene heaters. Test the tip-over before use where the manual tells you how.
Set up the fresh-air opening the label or manual gives before you light it, and put a working CO alarm in the room and where people sleep (safety_carbon_monoxide).
If the label is missing, burned off or unreadable, or the manual is lost and you cannot identify the model, treat the heater as outdoor only.
steps.warn: Burning any fuel heater inside without the air its maker asks for can kill everyone in the room.

notes:
## The words that matter
| The label says | What it means | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Not for home or recreational vehicle use | A construction heater: temporary heat for buildings under construction, with big fresh-air openings (Remington GFA, Deere HR-18R, Mr. Heater MHC) | Torpedo heaters, propane forced-air, cabinet propane heaters for sites |
| Not for use in homes, RVs or tents | Same, stated more plainly (Deere HR-18R) | |
| Outdoor use only / for outdoor use | Never inside a room, garage, tent or vehicle | Patio heaters, the Canada-sale Portable Buddy (Mr. Heater MH9BX CAN) |
| Indoor use / indoor safe / emergency indoor use | Rated for rooms, but only with the stated ventilation (Mr. Heater MH9BX, CPSC 5052) | Kerosene wick heaters, US Buddy heaters, catalytic heaters |
| Use only in well-ventilated areas | A condition, not a rating: it appears on indoor and construction heaters alike (Toyotomi KS-27A, Mr. Heater MH9BX, Deere HR-18R) | |
| Unvented | Every bit of exhaust stays in the room (Mr. Heater MH9BX) | |
| Direct-fired | All combustion products go into the heated space (Mr. Heater MHC, Remington GFA) | Torpedo and forced-air construction heaters |
| Indirect-fired | Exhaust leaves through a flue to outside (CSA B140.8) | Larger site and building-drying heaters |

'Residential' on a Mr. Heater product means safe in a home where local rules allow it, and the FAQ says Massachusetts and Canada do not allow propane heaters indoors and that California bars the Buddy series from dwellings (Mr. Heater FAQ). That is the maker's broad statement, not a quoted rule. The Canadian rule that can be quoted is BC's: gas-fired heaters used indoors must be vented to the outdoors, and propane cylinders are not permitted in a confined space, including enclosed tents (BC Safety Authority IB-GA 2017-01). The Canada-sale Buddy manual says outdoor use only, never in a home, camper, tent or car (Mr. Heater MH9BX CAN).

## Marks
A certification mark means samples were tested to a named standard and the product is listed in that lab's directory (Intertek ETL guide). It covers the use on the label, nothing more.
- **ETL (Intertek):** 'us' alone means US standards only; 'c' alone, Canadian only; both means both (Intertek ETL guide).
- Ask whether the mark comes from a certification agency recognized in the province of use, such as CSA or ULC (Canadian Propane Association CO 101).
- Check for the Canadian indicator: a heater marked for the US only was not tested to the Canadian standard.

## Which standard covers what
| Standard | Covers |
|---|---|
| CSA B140.9.3 | Portable kerosene heaters up to 4,400 W, unvented, 1-K kerosene only (CSA B140.9.3) |
| UL 647 | Unvented kerosene-fired room heaters and portable heaters (UL 647) |
| CSA/ANSI Z83.7 / CSA 2.14 | Gas-fired construction heaters, natural gas and propane, up to 10,000,000 Btu/h; the 2011 edition covers direct-fired heaters for temporary heating of buildings under construction (CCN Z83.7, NRC Z83.7) |
| CSA B140.8 | Portable industrial oil-fired heaters, direct- or indirect-fired, vented or unvented, for buildings under construction and spot heating (CSA B140.8) |
| UL 733 | Oil-fired air heaters and oil-fired direct-fired heaters (UL 733) |
| ANSI Z83.26 / CSA 2.37 | Gas-fired outdoor infrared patio heaters (CCN Z83.26) |
| 'e' approval number | European vehicle type approval on parking heaters; Webasto's Air Top 2000 STC lists e1*2001/56*0022*00 for the heater (Webasto AT2000) |

The 2023 edition of the gas construction heater standard adds requirements for vents, heat exchangers, heater openings on indirect-fired heaters, combustion air and ventilation, and draft hoods; Intertek listings must move to it by 1 Aug. 2027 (Intertek Z83.7 update). A kerosene torpedo heater can be CSA-certified for 1-K kerosene and still be a construction heater (Mr. Heater MHC).

## The oxygen depletion sensor (ODS)
An ODS is a pilot flame aimed at a thermocouple. On the Deere HR-18R, if the oxygen level falls below 18 %, the flame no longer touches the thermocouple, the current stops and the heater shuts off (Deere HR-18R). That is one maker's figure for one heater: read your own manual for its trip point. How to spot one: a small pilot assembly with a spark electrode and thermocouple beside the burner, a PILOT position on the knob, and 'ODS' or 'oxygen depletion sensor' in the manual (Mr. Heater MH9BX). What it does not do:
- It watches oxygen, not carbon monoxide. Mr. Heater still says the Buddy can give off excessive CO without enough air, and never to run it while sleeping (Mr. Heater MH9BX).
- It does not look at the burner. Mr. Heater says dust, lint or spider webs in the burner or venturi tube make the flame roll out over the tile and can start a fire, and a control knob left between its marked positions gives poor combustion and more CO (Mr. Heater MH9BX). Deere says a yellow pilot tip means the burner needs cleaning (Deere HR-18R). A sensor that only watches oxygen (Deere HR-18R) will not tell you the burner is dirty, so each time you light it check that the pilot is blue and the tile glows orange with no visible flame (Mr. Heater MH9BX).
- It trips with altitude: Buddy heaters may shut off above about 2,100 m (7,000 ft) (Mr. Heater MH9BX).
- It does not make a heater indoor-rated: the Deere HR-18R has an ODS and a tip switch and is still not for homes, RVs or tents (Deere HR-18R).

## The tip-over switch
A small switch inside a gas heater that shuts it off when tipped past a set angle (Mr. Heater FAQ). Bumping the heater can trip it; relight if so (Mr. Heater MH9BX). Kerosene wick heaters use an automatic extinguisher instead, a pendulum that lowers the wick when the heater is jarred; check it every time the wick is changed (Toyotomi KS-27A).

## Look-alikes
- **Portable Buddy, US and Canadian versions.** The US MH9BX manual allows indoor use in small recreational enclosures with a window or roof vent and in commercial enclosures, and emergency indoor heating only when it runs on a disposable 1 lb cylinder; it needs a 58 cm² (9 sq in) vent opening, must not run while sleeping, and its notice says not for a dwelling home in California (Mr. Heater MH9BX). The Canada-sale MH9BX manual says the heater is for outdoor use only and never for use in an enclosed space such as a camper, tent, car or home (Mr. Heater MH9BX CAN). Both carry the name Portable Buddy and the model number MH9BX.
- **Cabinet propane heaters.** A wheeled cabinet with a 20 lb cylinder inside looks like a living-room heater. The Deere HR-18R is one, and its label says not for home use (Deere HR-18R).
- **Kerosene heaters.** A round wick heater is certified as a room heater (CSA B140.9.3, UL 647). A kerosene forced-air torpedo is direct-fired and never for areas normally lived in (Mr. Heater MHC). Both burn kerosene.
- **Catalytic heaters.** The wall-mounted Olympian Wave (optional leg stands make it portable) needs a room with at least 155 cm² (24 sq in) of free-air opening, and its manual warns that many codes do not allow portable cylinders larger than 2 lb water capacity inside structures (Camco Wave). Industrial catalytic panels are indoor-only but not for homes (CATCO IOM).
- **Diesel heaters.** A diesel air (parking) heater can sit inside a vehicle because its combustion air intake, exhaust and fuel inlet are located outside the vehicle (Espar D2/D4). One cheap all-in-one portable diesel heater, a Vevor XMZ-W-D3, was turned back at the UK border in 2025 because it lacked the warnings that it must run only in well-ventilated spaces, with CO the danger (OPSS Vevor 2511-0300).

## Common heater types
| Heater | Fuel | Indoors, by its label? | Air it needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kerosene wick, convection or radiant | 1-K kerosene | Yes, rated | Door open to the rest of the house; also a window open about 2.5 cm (1 in) if the door must be shut or the house is tight (CPSC 5052) |
| Portable Buddy, US version | Propane: 1 lb cylinder for emergency indoor use; a 20 lb cylinder on a hose, kept outdoors, only in a recreational or temporary work enclosure | US label: yes (not in a California dwelling), never while sleeping | 58 cm² (9 sq in) opening (Mr. Heater MH9BX) |
| Portable Buddy, Canada-sale version | Propane | No: outdoor use only | (Mr. Heater MH9BX CAN) |
| Catalytic propane (Olympian Wave) | Propane | Yes, with its opening | 155 cm² (24 sq in) free-air opening, better as two openings high and low (Camco Wave) |
| Propane forced-air and cabinet construction heaters | Propane | Not in homes, RVs or tents | About 2,800 cm² (3 sq ft) to outside per 100,000 Btu/h (Remington GFA, Deere HR-18R) |
| Kerosene or diesel forced-air torpedo | Kerosene, diesel, fuel oil | Not where people live | 0.19 m² (2 sq ft) to outside near the floor and the same near the ceiling (Mr. Heater MHC) |
| Diesel air (parking) heater | Diesel | Only with intake and exhaust piped outside | Combustion air intake and exhaust piped outside the vehicle (Espar D2/D4) |
| Patio heater | Propane or natural gas | No, outdoor heater (CCN Z83.26) | |
| Camp stove, grill, generator, gas oven | Various | Never for heat | See [CO](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide) |

Mr. Heater says Canada does not allow propane heaters indoors (Mr. Heater FAQ), and BC's gas authority requires gas-fired heaters used indoors to be vented to the outdoors (BC Safety Authority IB-GA 2017-01). The US Buddy manual is marked 'for US sale except Massachusetts' (Mr. Heater MH9BX), so in Canada treat every Buddy as outdoor only. Every 'yes' above still needs a working CO alarm.
